# Yorkshire Dales National Park

Scroll down


## Dry Stone Walls & Waterfalls

The Yorkshire Dales has many moods; it can be wild and windswept or quietly tranquil with valleys full of hay meadows, dry stone walls and barns.

Spectacular waterfalls and ancient woodlands contrast with the scattered remains of rural industries. Together, nature and people created a special landscape of immense beauty and character – one of the most picturesque places in the country.

- [yorkshire\_dales](https://twitter.com/yorkshire_dales)
- [yorkshiredales](https://facebook.com/yorkshiredales)
- [yorkshiredales](https://instagram.com/yorkshiredales)

[yorkshiredales.org.uk](https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/)

## Key activities

There’s always something to do in the Dales. Whether you’re coming for the day or staying longer, there’s always lots going on

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/2.-Walkers-at-Malham-Stephen-Garnett-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Walking , Activity

Grab your boots and come and walk the Dales. There are walks to suit all ages and experience, including ‘miles without stiles’ accessible walks, hill and meadow walks.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/3.-Hardraw-Force-Wendy-McDonnell-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Waterfalls , Activity

You’ll find some of the finest limestone scenery in the UK. From pavements to caves to cascading waterfalls that plummet down dramatic cliff faces. There are dozens to visit.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/4.-Cheese-Stephen-Garnett-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Food & Drink , Activity

The Dales is perfect for foodies. There are cheese festivals, farmer markets, micro-breweries, and the world-famous Wensleydale Creamery in Hawes. Make sure you come hungry.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/5.-A-herd-of-sheep-Hill-Top-Farm-1920x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

10 reasons why the Yorkshire Dales is a special place…

Ancient dry-stone walls and field barns are defining features of the Dales landscape – shaped over thousands of years by people and nature. The iconic pattern of barns and walls in Upper Swaledale is recognised as being one of the most distinctive agricultural landscapes in Western Europe.

There are dozens of spectacular waterfalls such as Hardraw Force – the longest unbroken drop in England – Ingleton Falls, Janet’s Foss and the world famous Aysgarth Falls which featured alongside Hardraw Force in the hit movie ‘Robin Hood Prince of Thieves’.

The Yorkshire Dales has some of the most spectacular peaks in England, and the famous Yorkshire Three Peaks of Whernside, Ingleborough and Pen-y-Ghent are amongst the highest in the county, providing an inspiring challenge to walkers from around the world.

Yorkshire is the home of cycling thanks to the 2014 Tour de France ‘Grand Depart’ and Le Tour de Yorkshire. The Dales offers some of the best cycling the country – from gentle routes in the valleys to challenging climbs over the moorland that separates them; including the iconic Buttertubs pass. Check out cyclethedales.org.uk

Over a quarter of England’s flower-rich upland hay meadows and pastures are here – outstanding examples can be found in Swaledale and Langstrothdale – and keep an eye out for nationally important populations of birds like curlew, lapwing, and black grouse.

Some of the best examples of classic limestone scenery can be found the Yorkshire Dales. With its scars such as those at Gordale and Attermire and limestone pavements such as those at Great Asby Scar and Malham Cove, which featured in ‘Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows part two’.

The most extensive caving area in the UK is here, including the longest cave system – the Three Counties System – and one of the largest caverns and the highest unbroken underground waterfall at Gaping Gill.

The stunning dark sky of the Yorkshire Dales National Park is one of its very special qualities, and each year we support a special festival to celebrate it. The Dark Sky Festival is all about discovering, learning and enjoying the galaxies and stars you don’t normally get to see.

Around 42% of the area of the National Park is moorland, which is internationally important for wildlife, plant species and the carbon they store as peat.

Livestock farming – with distinct sheep breeds like Wensleydale and Swaledale and a strong tradition of upland cattle rearing, that is still deeply interwoven into local life and made famous through local cheese making. Livestock sales and agricultural shows play an important part in the lives of local people.

## Did you know?

There are over 8,000km of dry-stone walls and 6,000 field barns in the Yorkshire Dales National Park and half the country’s limestone pavements.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/6.-Belties-Paul-Harris-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/7.-Heather-Wendy-McDonnell-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/8.-Kids-lunching-Stephen-Garnett--900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/9.-Red-Squirrel-Gaz-Atkinson-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/10.-Kids-in-stream-at-Malham-Stephen-Garnett-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/11.-Steam-Train-Paul-Harris-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/12.-Pen-y-Ghent-Andy-Kay-900x600.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/13.-DentHead-Paul-Harris-900x600.jpg)

## Enjoying the Yorkshire Dales

There are many ways to enjoy the Yorkshire Dales! Whether you’re coming by car, train, bike or on foot, whether you’re coming for the day or staying for longer.

One of the best ways in which you can enjoy the Dales is by walking; there are over 60 varied [short walks](https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/things-to-do/get-outdoors/walking/short-walks/) you can take to enjoy the wonderful scenery. If you fancy more of a challenge, there are [longer distance](https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/things-to-do/get-outdoors/walking/long-distance/) options which include the Pennine Way, Coast to Coast,  Pennine Bridleway, and the famous Three Peaks, where the aim is to walk 24 miles, covering all three summits, Pen-y-Ghent, Whernside and Ingleborough, in 12 hours!

Other ways to access the Dales are [cycling](https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/things-to-do/get-outdoors/cycling/) and [mountain biking](https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/things-to-do/get-outdoors/adventure-activities/mountain-biking/) – a great way to take in the landscape and observe the wildlife. We have a network of 900km of bridleways, by-ways and [green lanes](https://www.yorkshiredales.org.uk/things-to-do/get-outdoors/where-can-i-go/green-lanes/) available for you to use, or try some of the Tour de France and Tour de Yorkshire routes. There are plenty of picture postcard towns and villages to stop off for refreshments!

Take a heritage train journey on the iconic Settle – Carlisle line which cuts through the heart of the Dales, providing stunning views of the landscape and taking in famous features such as the Ribblehead viaduct and the Westmorland fells or take the Wensleydale Railway from Leaming to Redmire.

Stay a while, there are hundreds of cosy B&B’s and holiday cottages to suit everyone. Bring friends, bring families, and enjoy everything the Yorkshire Dales has to offer.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Ribblehead-Image-Yorkshire-Dales-1840x1080.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/15.-Cycling-Paul-Harris-580x580.jpg)

### Getting around

The Yorkshire Dales National Park is very accessible by road, but there are lots of alternative, greener ways to get about including walking, cycling and taking the train or bus.

The excellent DalesBus network through the Yorkshire Dales National Park offers wonderful opportunities for sightseeing and walking. And in the north of the Park, the community run Little White bus links Garsdale station to Hawes, and there are services from Richmond, Leyburn and Reeth.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/16.-Horseriding-Paul-Harris-580x580.jpg)

### Getting there

If you’re coming by car, the M6 skirts the National Park to the west, the A66 to the north, the A1 to the east and the A65 and A59 to the south.

By train you can access the Dales from Northallerton, or Darlington on the East Coast mainline with bus connections into places like Leyburn, Hawes and Reeth. Or you can travel directly into the heart of the Dales on one of the scheduled services from Leeds to Carlisle using the iconic Settle – Carlisle line. Services stop in Settle, Horton in Ribblesdale, Ribblehead, Garsdale and Kirkby Stephen.

Taking the bus is an excellent way of enjoying the views without having to worry about keeping your eyes on the road. It helps reduce congestion and parking problems. Visit [www.dalesbus.org](http://www.dalesbus.org/) or [www.traveline.info](http://www.traveline.info/)

# Long distance routes

Long distance trails give you a fantastic sense of achievement. Baggage handlers can lighten your load and organise accommodation, or you can complete the route in stages using public transport.

* * *

## 100 – 270 miles

### Pennine Way

The oldest and most iconic National Trail offers a rugged taste of Northern England – stretching from the Peak District to the Scottish Borders on a challenging but rewarding route of remarkable contrasts. With a combined ascent that exceeds the height of Mount Everest, the Pennine Way is arguably the most challenging National Trail in England and the route is recommended for experienced walkers who want a unique experience – but you don’t have to walk it all at once.

[Click here for more information](https://www.nationaltrail.co.uk/pennine-way)

Length: 268 miles

### Coast to Coast Path

This particularly challenging route passes through three stunning national parks: the Lake District National Park, the Yorkshire Dales National Park, and the North York Moors National Park. However because of this unique route, walkers will witness some of the most stunning natural sights England has to offer as it takes you across beautiful valleys, hills and mountains.

Length: 192 miles

### Pennine Bridleway

The Pennine bridleway is specifically designed for the use by equestrians however it is a good challenge for cyclists. The route follows a variety of surfaces including minor roads, aggregate tracks, grassed stone tracks, stone setts and worn causey flags. Some of these have been newly created specifically for the Pennine Bridleway but some are ancient highways such as drovers roads or packhorse trails that have been in use for centuries.

[Click here for more information](https://www.nationaltrail.co.uk/pennine-bridleway)

Length: 205 miles

### Pennine Journey

The Pennine Journey is a challenging walk taking place mostly in the north Pennines area, however some of it takes place in the beautiful Yorkshire dales national park, including the starting in the town of Settle. The Pennine Journey is one of three looped walks but it is by far the biggest loop.

[Click here for more information](http://www.penninejourney.org.uk/)

Length: 247 miles

* * *

## 80 – 100 miles

### Lady Anne’s Way

This route was inspired by Lady Anne Clifford, that Lady who owned vast estates in the seventeenth century. Lady Anne was known to travel between her castles and this route takes in these beautiful buildings, most of which are now ruins. This walk starts in the lovely town of Skipton in the Yorkshire Dales National Park and ends in the charming town of Penrith in Cumbria’s Eden Valley.

[Click here for more information](http://www.ladyannesway.co.uk/)

Length: 100 miles

### Dales High Way

The Dales Highways is a high level route through the Dales and containing summits of Ingleborough, Whernside, the Howgills, Ilkley Moor and Sharp Haw but most of the route keeps to high ground. The Dales Highway is for the more experienced walker but you can always make it easy by creating your own route or breaking it down into easier sections.

[Click for here more information](https://www.daleshighway.co.uk/)

Length: 90 miles

### Dales Way

The Dales Way runs for 80 miles from Ilkley in West Yorkshire to Bowness-on-Windermere. This route follows mostly riverside paths, passing through the Yorkshire Dales National Park and the gentle foothills of southern Lakeland to the shore of England’s most famous lake, Lake Windermere.

[Click here for more information](http://www.dalesway.org/route.html)

Length: 80 miles

* * *

## 50 – 80 miles

### Herriot Way

This beautiful route takes place in the heart of the Yorkshire Dales National Park, visiting many locations that were used in the filming of the TV programme ‘All Creatures Great & Small’. This programme is based on a series of book written by the veterinary surgeon Alf Wight under the pseudonym James Herriot in the 1970s. This pleasant route is done in four days starting in any location you would like eventually bringing back where you started.

[Click here for more information](http://www.herriotway.com/)

Length: 52 miles

### Ribble Way

As you can probably guess by its name the Ribble Way follows the River Ribble starting from its mouth at Longton, near Preston, to the source at Gayle Moor in Yorkshire. The route goes from Lancashire into Yorkshire before passing through the gorgeous Yorkshire Dales national park and finishing at the source at Gavel Moor near Ribblehead and the famous Ribblehead Viaduct.

[Click here for more information](https://www.ldwa.org.uk/ldp/members/show_path.php?path_name=Ribble+Way)

Length: 70 miles

### Dales Inn Way

The walk is divided into six stages and passes 26 traditional Dales inns, with each stage consisting of around 13 miles of route each. The route starts and finishes in Grassington as it is a circular route taking you to beautiful towns and villages like Reeth, Askrigg and Buckden with many more along the way.

[Click for here more information](http://www.innway.co.uk/the-inn-way-walking-books/the-inn-way-to-the-yorkshire-dales.html)

Length: 76 miles

## 20 – 50 miles

### Kirkby Stephen Cycle

A great route for exploring the north west corner of the Yorkshire Dales National Park. The route combines sections of quiet road with tracks, byways and some bridleways across open fell. Watch out for the Helm Wind, a strong north easterly which blows down from Cross Fell and is the only named wind in Britain.

This part of the national park is popular with walkers due to the presence of the [Yorkshire three peaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_three_peaks "Yorkshire three peaks"). The **Yorkshire Dales National Park** is a 2,178km2 (841sqmi) [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_England_and_Wales "National parks of England and Wales") in England which covers most of the [Yorkshire Dales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales "Yorkshire Dales"), the [Howgill Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howgill_Fells "Howgill Fells"), and the [Orton Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orton_Fells "Orton Fells"). The [Nidderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nidderdale "Nidderdale") area of the Yorkshire Dales is not within the national park, and has instead been designated a [national landscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Landscape "National Landscape"). Most of the park is within [North Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Yorkshire "North Yorkshire"), with a sizeable area in [Cumbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumbria "Cumbria") and a small part in [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire"). The park was designated in 1954, and extended in 2016. More than 95% of the land in the park is privately owned; there are over 1,000 farms in this area.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-1) In 2020, the national park was named an [International Dark Sky Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Dark-Sky_Association "International Dark-Sky Association"). This means the park has "low levels of [light pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_pollution "Light pollution"), ideal conditions for [stargazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargazing "Stargazing") and [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy")".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-2) As of 2017,[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park&action=edit) some 23,500 residents live within the park boundary; a 2018 report estimated that the park attracted more than four million visitors per year.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-3) The economy consists primarily of tourism and agriculture.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-4) ## Location The park is 50 miles (80km) north-east of [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"); [Otley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otley "Otley"), [Ilkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilkley "Ilkley"), [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds") and [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford "Bradford") lie to the south, while [Kendal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendal "Kendal") is to the west, [Darlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlington "Darlington") to the north-east and [Harrogate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrogate "Harrogate") to the south-east.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-5) The national park does not include all the Yorkshire Dales. Parts of the dales to the south and east of the national park are located in the [Nidderdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nidderdale_Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty "Nidderdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty"). The national park includes the [Howgill Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howgill_Fells "Howgill Fells") and [Orton Fells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orton_Fells "Orton Fells") in the north-west although they are not often considered part of the Dales.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ## History ### Creation In 1947, the [Hobhouse Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Hobhouse "Arthur Hobhouse") recommended the creation of the Yorkshire Dales National Park covering parts of the [West Riding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Riding "West Riding") and [North Riding of Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Riding_of_Yorkshire "North Riding of Yorkshire"). The proposed National Park included most of the Yorkshire Dales, but not [Nidderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nidderdale "Nidderdale"). Accordingly, Nidderdale was not included in the National Park when it was designated in 1954. In 1963 the then [West Riding County Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Riding_County_Council "West Riding County Council") proposed that Nidderdale should be added to the National Park, but the proposal met with opposition from the [district councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_District_Council "Rural District Council") which would have lost some of their powers to the county council. Following the [Local Government Act 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Government_Act_1972 "Local Government Act 1972") most of the area of the national park was transferred in 1974 to the new county of North Yorkshire. An area in the north west of the national park ( [Dentdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentdale "Dentdale"), [Garsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garsdale "Garsdale") and the town of [Sedbergh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedbergh "Sedbergh")) was transferred from the West Riding of Yorkshire to the new county of Cumbria. In 1997 management of the national park passed from the county councils to the Yorkshire Dales National Park Authority.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-6) ### 2016 extension A westward extension of the park into [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") and [Westmorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmorland "Westmorland") encompassed much of the area between the old boundaries of the park and the [M6 motorway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M6_motorway "M6 motorway"). This increased the area by nearly 24% and brought the park close to the towns of [Kirkby Lonsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkby_Lonsdale "Kirkby Lonsdale"), [Kirkby Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkby_Stephen "Kirkby Stephen") and [Appleby-in-Westmorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleby-in-Westmorland "Appleby-in-Westmorland").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-11) The extension also includes the northern portion of the Howgill Fells and most of the Orton Fells.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-12) The expansion brought in parts of historic [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") and [Westmorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westmorland "Westmorland") to join part of North Yorkshire and the south-western part of Cumbria. ## Tourism [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Pub_bullshead_Hawes_177.jpg/500px-Pub_bullshead_Hawes_177.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pub_bullshead_Hawes_177.jpg) A traditional hotel in Hawes The area has a wide range of activities for visitors. For example, many people come to the Dales for walking or other exercise. Several long-distance routes cross the park, including the [Pennine Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennine_Way "Pennine Way"), the [Dales Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dales_Way "Dales Way"), the [Coast to Coast Walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_to_Coast_Walk "Coast to Coast Walk") and the [Pennine Bridleway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennine_Bridleway "Pennine Bridleway").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-13) Cycling is also popular and there are several cycleways.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-14) The [DalesBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DalesBus "DalesBus") service provides service in the Dales on certain days in summer, "including the Yorkshire Dales National Park and Nidderdale Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty". In summer, these buses supplement the other services that operate year-round in the Dales.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-16) Tourism in the region declined due to restrictions necessitated by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") in 2020, and into 2021. Later in 2021, the volume of visits was expected to increase as a result of the 2020 TV series _[All Creatures Great and Small](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Creatures_Great_and_Small_(2020_TV_series) "All Creatures Great and Small (2020 TV series)")_, largely filmed within the Dales.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales_National_Park#cite_note-17) The first series aired in the UK in September 2020 and in the US in early 2021.
